steps.body: The 1 at $B = 0, C = 0$ gives $\overline{B}\,\overline{C}$ (true for both values of $A$).

steps.body: The entry $A$ at $(1, 1)$: its neighbours are $(0, 1) = 0$ and $(1, 0) = \overline{A}$ (which cannot join an $A$-loop), so it stays alone: $BC$, giving $A \cdot BC = ABC$.

steps.title: The A′ pass
steps.body: The entry $\overline{A}$ at $(1, 0)$ may join the 1 at $(0, 0)$ (same column $C = 0$): the loop $\overline{C}$, giving $\overline{A}\,\overline{C}$.

steps.body: Unfolded over $(A, B, C)$: $m_0, m_4$ (from the 1), $m_2$ (from $\overline{A}$ at $B = 1, C = 0$), $m_7$ (from $A$ at $B = C = 1$): $f = \Sigma(0, 2, 4, 7)$. Its K-map loops are exactly $\overline{B}\,\overline{C}$, $\overline{A}\,\overline{C}$ and $ABC$, all essential.

Detecting $t$ errors requires $d_{min}\ge t+1$, so 3-bit detection needs $d_{min}=4$. Adding one overall parity bit to Hamming(7,4) gives the extended (8,4) code with $d_{min}=4$.

Extra parity bits $=3+1=4$; minimum distance $=4$.

steps.title: (a) is valid
steps.body: If $\forall x\,P(x)$ holds, then every $x$ satisfies $P(x) \lor Q(x)$; likewise if $\forall x\,Q(x)$ holds. Either way $\forall x\,\{P(x) \lor Q(x)\}$.

steps.title: Counter-models for (b), (c)

Domain $\{1, 2\}$, $P = \{1\}$, $Q = \{2\}$.

- (b): $\exists P$ and $\exists Q$ are true, but no element has both, so $\exists(P \land Q)$ is false.
- (c): every element is in $P$ or $Q$, so $\forall(P \lor Q)$ is true, but neither $\forall P$ nor $\forall Q$ holds.

- (a) $a = 1, b = 0$: $a \lor b = 1$, $b \land c = 0$ → false.
- (c) $a = b = 1, c = 0$: $1 \to (1 \to 0) = 1 \to 0 = 0$.
- (d) $a = b = 1, c = 0$: either grouping gives $0$ — right-associated $1 \to (1 \to 0) = 0$; left-associated $(1 \to 1) \to (1 \to 0) = 1 \to 0 = 0$.

steps.body: NFA → DFA by the subset construction (at most $2^n$ states). An NTM is simulated by a DTM that explores its computation tree breadth-first, accepting the same language.

steps.title: Sorted input
steps.body: Input $1, 2, \dots, n$. Pivot $= n$ (largest): all others go left, right part empty. Recursion on $1, \dots, n-1$ again picks the largest, and so on.

steps.body: LRU and optimal are stack algorithms: the pages held with k frames are always a subset of those held with k+1 frames, so faults can never increase.

cse-1992-b-4-a.approach: Concept tested: **the overflow condition**. Overflow is about the signed range, not about the carry out: it happens exactly when the carry into the sign bit differs from the carry out of it, i.e. when two same-sign operands give a result of the other sign.
concepts: Carry into vs out of the MSB

steps.title: Why a carry is not enough
steps.body: In 2's complement the carry out of the MSB is discarded: $-1 + 1 = 1111 + 0001 = 1\,0000$ gives the correct 0 with a carry. So 'carry out' cannot mean overflow.

steps.title: The condition
steps.body: Overflow $\iff c_{n-1} \oplus c_n = 1$ (carry into the sign column ≠ carry out of it) $\iff$ both operands have the same sign and the result's sign differs.

steps.title: Why it holds
steps.body: Both non-negative: $c_n = 0$, and overflow means the sign bit became 1, which needs $c_{n-1} = 1$. Both negative: $c_n = 1$, and overflow means the sign bit became 0, which needs $c_{n-1} = 0$. Mixed signs never overflow and always have $c_{n-1} = c_n$.

answer.value: Overflow iff the carry into the MSB differs from the carry out of the MSB (equivalently, both operands have the same sign and the result's sign differs)

pitfalls: Writing 'overflow when there is a carry out of the MSB'.
Forgetting that opposite signs never overflow.
cse-1992-b-4-a.verification: $0101 + 0100 = 1001$: carries in/out of the MSB are 1/0, and $5 + 4 = 9$ does overflow. ✓

steps.body: 3-bit Gray sequence $000 \to 001 \to 011 \to 010 \to 110 \to 111 \to 101 \to 100 \to 000$. Since $D = Q^{+}$, the D columns equal the next state.

steps.body: Three D flip-flops on a common clock with the inputs above (two AND-OR networks and one XNOR). Each transition flips exactly one bit, including the wrap-around $100 \to 000$.

steps.body: Priority of A > B > C must follow the line priorities, so A drives INTR1, B drives INTR2 and C drives INTR3.

steps.title: Masking
steps.body: Mask register bits $M_1, M_2, M_3$ (set by software). Effective requests: $I_1 = R_A M_1$, $I_2 = R_B M_2$, $I_3 = R_C M_3$. A masked device cannot interrupt even if it requests.

steps.body:
$$G_A = I_1,\quad G_B = \overline{I_1}\,I_2,\quad G_C = \overline{I_1}\,\overline{I_2}\,I_3$$
$$\text{INT} = \text{IEN}\cdot(I_1 + I_2 + I_3)$$
The grants (or a priority encoder with outputs $x y$) form the vector address placed on the bus when the CPU acknowledges.

cse-1992-b-6-a.approach: Split the 1 MB space into four 256 KB quadrants with $A_{19}A_{18}$ — each big device (256 KB EPROM, 256 KB RAM) then needs exactly one decoder output, and the small EERAM and I/O share one quadrant with partial decoding. This minimises decoding logic.

steps.title: Count the chips
steps.body: $\frac{256\text{K}}{256\text{K}} = 1$ EPROM, $\frac{256\text{K}}{64\text{K}} = 4$ RAM chips, $\frac{1\text{K}}{256} = 4$ EERAM chips. The printed "6 K × 8" must be 64 K × 8 ($256/6$ is not an integer and 6 K is not a power of two).

steps.title: Quadrants from A19 A18
steps.body:
$2^{20} = 1\text{M}$ and $256\text{K} = 2^{18}$, so $A_{19}A_{18}$ picks a quadrant through one 2-to-4 decoder (enabled only for memory cycles, $IO/\overline{M}=0$):

| $A_{19}A_{18}$ | Range | Device |
|---|---|---|
| 00 | 00000–3FFFF | EPROM (reset address 0 lies in ROM, as on an 8085) |
| 01 | 40000–7FFFF | RAM |
| 10 | 80000–BFFFF | EERAM + I/O |
| 11 | C0000–FFFFF | free |

$Y_0$ drives the EPROM $\overline{CS}$ directly.

steps.title: RAM bank select
steps.body:
$Y_1$ enables a second 2-to-4 decoder on $A_{17}A_{16}$:
RAM0 40000–4FFFF, RAM1 50000–5FFFF, RAM2 60000–6FFFF, RAM3 70000–7FFFF. Each chip gets $A_{15}$–$A_0$ and $D_7$–$D_0$.

steps.title: EERAM and I/O share quadrant 10

Use $A_{17}$ to split $Y_2$:

- $Y_2\cdot\overline{A_{17}}$ enables a 2-to-4 decoder on $A_9A_8$ → EERAM0–3 at 80000–800FF, 80100–801FF, 80200–802FF, 80300–803FF (chips get $A_7$–$A_0$).
- $Y_2\cdot A_{17}$ enables a 4-to-16 decoder on $A_3$–$A_0$ → I/O devices 0–15 at A0000–A000F.

Lines $A_{16}$, $A_{15}$–$A_{10}$ (EERAM) and $A_{16}$–$A_4$ (I/O) are left undecoded: the devices simply repeat (fold back) inside their region, which is harmless since that region holds nothing else.

steps.body: Three 2-to-4 decoders, one 4-to-16 decoder and two AND/inverter gates for $A_{17}$ — no comparator on the high address lines is needed because every boundary falls on a $2^{k}$ boundary.

cse-1992-b-6-b.approach: Compare the access time the CPU gives (two clock cycles) with the EERAM read and write times, then stretch only EERAM cycles by pulling the 8085-style READY line low for the required number of wait states, counted by a small counter.

steps.title: Time the CPU provides
steps.body:
$T = \frac{1}{12.5\ \text{MHz}} = 80\ \text{ns}$, so a normal access gets $2T = 160\ \text{ns}$.
RAM (140 ns) and EPROM (150 ns) fit; EERAM (500 ns read, 3 µs write) does not.

steps.title: Wait states needed
steps.body:
Each wait state adds one $T$.

- Read: $\lceil (500-160)/80 \rceil = \lceil 4.25 \rceil = 5$ → $7 \times 80 = 560\ \text{ns} \ge 500$.
- Write: $\lceil (3000-160)/80 \rceil = \lceil 35.5 \rceil = 36$ → $38 \times 80 = 3040\ \text{ns} \ge 3000$.

steps.title: Extra logic
steps.body:
- A 6-bit synchronous counter clocked by CLK, held cleared while $\overline{CS}_{EERAM}$ (the $Y_2\cdot\overline{A_{17}}$ decoder output of part (a)) is inactive.
- When an EERAM cycle starts (CS active with $\overline{RD}$ or $\overline{WR}$ low) the counter counts clock cycles.
- $READY = \overline{CS_{EERAM}} + \overline{RD}{=}0 \cdot (\text{count} \ge 5) + \overline{WR}{=}0 \cdot (\text{count} \ge 36)$, i.e. READY stays low (CPU inserts $T_W$ states) until the count reaches 5 for a read or 36 for a write; then READY goes high and the cycle completes.
- All other devices leave READY high, so they run with no wait states.

answer.value: Clock period 80 ns, so 160 ns is available; EERAM needs 5 wait states for a read (7 × 80 = 560 ns ≥ 500 ns) and 36 for a write (38 × 80 = 3040 ns ≥ 3 µs), produced by a counter that holds READY low while the EERAM chip select is active

Using the read count for writes: the 3 µs write dominates.

cse-1992-b-7-a.approach: Trace one call: the inner loop just counts up to $F(n-1)$, so $C = F(n-1)$, and the outer loop multiplies $F1$ by that value $n$ times.

steps.title: Base case
steps.body: For $n = 1$ the function returns $F = 3$, so $F(1) = 3$.

steps.title: Inner loop
steps.body: For a fixed $i$: $C$ starts at 0 and is incremented once per iteration of $j = 1 \ldots F(n-1)$, so after the loop $C = F(n-1)$.

steps.title: Outer loop
steps.body:
$F1$ starts at 1 and is multiplied by $C = F(n-1)$ for each $i = 1 \ldots n$:
$$F1 = \underbrace{F(n-1)\cdot F(n-1)\cdots F(n-1)}_{n\ \text{times}} = F(n-1)^{n}.$$
Hence
$$F(1)=3,\qquad F(n) = F(n-1)^{\,n}\ \ (n > 1).$$

pitfalls: Writing $F(n) = n\cdot F(n-1)$ — the loop multiplies by $C$, not adds.

cse-1992-b-7-b.approach: Take logarithms base 3: the exponent $e(n) = \log_3 F(n)$ satisfies $e(n) = n\,e(n-1)$ with $e(1) = 1$, which is the factorial.

steps.title: Write F as a power of 3
Unroll
steps.body: $e(n) = n\,(n-1)\,e(n-2) = \cdots = n(n-1)\cdots 2\cdot e(1) = n!$

steps.title: Closed form
steps.body:
Substituting $e(n) = n!$ back into $F(n) = 3^{e(n)}$:
$$F(n) = 3^{\,n!}$$

pitfalls: Answering $3^n$ or $3^{n^2}$ — the exponent multiplies, it does not add.

cse-1992-b-8.approach: In a DFS of an undirected graph every non-tree edge is a back edge, so one endpoint is an ancestor of the other and the cycle is that tree path plus $(u,v)$. Since we do not know which endpoint is the ancestor, climb from both in lock-step; whichever climb hits the other endpoint first has taken exactly the path length $d$ steps, so the work is $O(d)$.

steps.title: Shape of the cycle
steps.body: Undirected DFS has no cross edges: for $(u,v) \in G - T$, either $v$ is an ancestor of $u$ or vice versa. Adding $(u,v)$ closes the cycle (descendant → parent → … → ancestor → descendant).

steps.title: Find the ancestor in O(d)
steps.body: Set $x := u$, $y := v$ and repeat $x := P[x]$, $y := P[y]$ until $x = v$ or $y = u$. If $v$ is $d$ levels above $u$, $x$ reaches $v$ after $d$ steps; $y$ climbs at most $d$ steps too (stopping harmlessly at the root since $P[root] = root$). So both loops cost $O(d)$ and $d + 1$ is the cycle length.

steps.title: Algorithm
Cost
steps.body: Both while-loops run at most $d$ times where $d$ = depth difference of $u$ and $v$; the cycle has $d+1$ edges, so time is $\Theta(\text{cycle length})$.

answer.value: In a DFS tree a non-tree edge joins an ancestor and a descendant: follow P[] from the descendant up to the ancestor, printing each vertex, then close with the edge back (climb from u and v in lock-step to find which is the descendant; O(cycle length))

pitfalls: Climbing only from $u$ to the root and checking for $v$ — if $u$ is the ancestor this walks to the root, not $O(\text{cycle})$.
Using depth arrays or marking — not given and may cost more than the cycle.
cse-1992-b-8.verification: Example: tree path r–a–b–c with back edge (c, a): x climbs c→b→a = v after 2 steps; y climbs a→r→r; printed cycle c b a c has 3 edges = d + 1.

cse-1992-b-9.approach: Use the classic sparse-set: a dense array of members with a count, plus a position array indexed by value. Membership is a two-way cross-check, so even the position array may hold garbage — only the count needs initialising.

steps.title: Structure and initialisation
steps.body:
- $E[1..n]$: the members of $S$ stored compactly in $E[1..k]$.
- $pos[1..n]$: $pos[x]$ = index of $x$ in $E$ (meaningful only if $x \in S$).
- $k$: current size.

Assumption: only $k := 0$ is initialised; $E$ and $pos$ may contain arbitrary values.

steps.title: Routines (all O(1))
Why it is correct
steps.body: A garbage $pos[x]$ cannot fake membership: if $x \notin S$, any $p$ in $1..k$ has $E[p]$ = some member $\ne x$. DELETE moves the last member into the hole, keeping $E[1..k]$ dense. Example: DELETE(6) → $E = [7, 2]$, $pos[7] = 1$, $k = 2$.

answer.value: Two arrays: dense list E[1..n] of members with a count k, and pos[1..n] giving each member's index in E; delete swaps the last element into the vacated slot

pitfalls: A plain bit vector gives MEMBER/ADD/DELETE in O(1) but FIND-ONE needs a scan.
Forgetting to update $pos$ of the moved element on delete.
cse-1992-b-9.verification: Each routine performs a fixed number of array accesses independent of |S| and n; the invariant pos[E[i]] = i for 1 ≤ i ≤ k is preserved by ADD and DELETE.

cse-1992-b-10-a.approach: Copy in at entry, work on a local copy, copy back at exit — that is copy-restore (call-by-value-result). The flaw is that step 4 re-evaluates the l-value $A[i]$ at exit, so if $i$ changes inside $P$ the result is written to the wrong element.

steps.title: Identify the mechanism
steps.body: Steps 1–2 copy the actual's value into a local ($z := A[i]$), step 3 uses only the copy, step 4 copies the value back. That is **call-by-value-result** (copy-in/copy-out).

steps.title: What goes wrong
steps.body: In value-result the address of the actual parameter is fixed **at call time**. Step 4 evaluates $A[i]$ again **at return**. If $P$ modifies the global $i$ (e.g. $i := i + 1$), $z$ is stored into $A[i_{new}]$, not into the element that was passed. Example: $i = 1$, $P$ sets $z := 5$ and $i := 2$ ⇒ the given code changes $A[2]$; value-result should change $A[1]$.

steps.title: Minimal correction
steps.body:
Save the address (or index) at entry and use it at exit:

1. Create local $z$ (and $j$ / pointer $p$).
2. $j := i$ (or $p := \&A[i]$); $z := A[j]$.
3. Execute $P$ using $z$ for the parameter.
4. $A[j] := z$ (or $*p := z$).

answer.value: Call-by-value-result; incorrect if i changes inside P — the address of A[i] must be computed once at call time (e.g. j := i or a pointer) and step 4 must store z into that saved location

pitfalls: Calling it call-by-name: call-by-name would re-evaluate $A[i]$ at every use, not copy into $z$.
cse-1992-b-10-a.verification: If i is never changed inside P both versions behave identically, which confirms the only difference is the time of l-value evaluation.

cse-1992-b-10-b.approach: Resolve each call by static scope (the inner A declared in B shadows the outer A inside B), then stack activation records in call order; the display entry $d[k]$ points to the latest activation at static nesting depth $k$.
cse-1992-b-10-b.given:
| Procedure | Declared in | Nesting depth |
|---|---|---|
| Test | — | 1 |
| A (outer) | Test | 2 |
| B | A (outer) | 3 |
| A (inner) | B | 4 |

steps.title: Which A is called
steps.body: At $x$ (body of Test) only the outer A is visible → **A(outer)**. A(outer)'s body calls B. At $y$ (body of B) the inner A declared inside B shadows the outer one → **A(inner)**.

steps.title: Just after the call at x
steps.body:
Stack (bottom → top): **Test**, **A(outer)**.
Display: $d[1] \to$ Test, $d[2] \to$ A(outer). The AR of A(outer) saves the previous $d[2]$ (undefined).

steps.title: Just after the call at y
steps.body:
Call chain Test → A(outer) → B → A(inner). Stack: **Test**, **A(outer)**, **B**, **A(inner)**.
Display: $d[1] \to$ Test, $d[2] \to$ A(outer), $d[3] \to$ B, $d[4] \to$ A(inner). Each AR holds the saved old $d[k]$ for its level, the return address/control link and its locals.

scene.caption: At y: d[1..4] = Test, A(outer), B, A(inner)

answer.value: At x: stack Test, A(outer); display d[1]=Test, d[2]=A(outer). At y: stack Test, A(outer), B, A(inner); display d[1]=Test, d[2]=A(outer), d[3]=B, d[4]=A(inner)

pitfalls: Taking the call at y as a recursive call of the outer A — it refers to the inner A (depth 4).
cse-1992-b-10-b.verification: The display length equals the nesting depth of the running procedure: 2 at x (A outer), 4 at y (A inner).

cse-1992-b-11-a.approach: With rules allowed only at production ends, the type of $T$ cannot be passed down into $L$ (that would need an inherited attribute before $L$). So collect the identifiers into a synthesized list in $L$ and do all the symbol-table updates at the end of $D \to T L;$, where both $T.type$ and $L.list$ are available.

steps.title: Attributes
steps.body: $T.type$ (synthesized), $L.list$ (synthesized list of symbol-table entries), $id.entry$ (from the lexer). $addtype(e, t)$ records type $t$ in entry $e$.

steps.title: Semantic rules
steps.body:
| Production | Rule |
|---|---|
| $D \rightarrow T\,L\,;$ | for each $e$ in $L.list$: $addtype(e, T.type)$ |
| $T \rightarrow \text{int}$ | $T.type := integer$ |
| $T \rightarrow \text{real}$ | $T.type := real$ |
| $L \rightarrow L_1 , \text{id}$ | $L.list := append(L_1.list, id.entry)$ |
| $L \rightarrow \text{id}$ | $L.list := [\,id.entry\,]$ |

steps.title: Example
steps.body: For "real x, y;" : $L.list = [x, y]$, $T.type = real$, and the rule at the end of $D$ calls $addtype(x, real)$, $addtype(y, real)$.

answer.value: T → int {T.type := integer}; T → real {T.type := real}; L → id {L.list := [id.entry]}; L → L1 , id {L.list := L1.list + [id.entry]}; D → T L ; {for each e in L.list: addtype(e, T.type)}

pitfalls: Writing $L.in := T.type$ — that is an inherited attribute evaluated in the middle of $D \to TL;$, which the question forbids.
cse-1992-b-11-a.verification: Every rule uses only attributes of the production's right side and is placed at its end, so it is S-attributed and fits a bottom-up parse.

cse-1992-b-11-b.approach: Parenthesise by precedence (arithmetic > relational > and > or), then emit quadruples in post-order, left operand first; with no short-circuit, every comparison is computed as a value.

steps.title: Parse
steps.body:
Precedence: $+$ above relational ops, relational above **and**, **and** above **or**:
$$\big((a+b) > (c+d)\big)\ \textbf{or}\ \big((a>c)\ \textbf{and}\ (b<d)\big)$$

answer.value: t1 = a + b; t2 = c + d; t3 = t1 > t2; t4 = a > c; t5 = b < d; t6 = t4 and t5; t7 = t3 or t6

pitfalls: Generating jumps (short-circuit code) — the question forbids partial evaluation.
Grouping as $(\ldots \textbf{ or } a>c) \textbf{ and } b<d$ — and binds tighter than or.
cse-1992-b-11-b.verification: Seven operators in the expression ⇒ seven quadruples, each temporary used exactly once afterwards.

cse-1992-b-12-a.approach: Translate structurally: statements in sequence give a chain; a parbegin fans out from the statement before it to the first statement of every branch and fans in from the last statement of every branch to the statement after parend.

steps.title: Outer structure
steps.body:
$S_1$; parbegin [ $S_2;S_4$ ] ‖ [ $S_3$; parbegin $S_5$ ‖ [ $S_6;S_8$ ] parend ] ‖ $S_7$ parend; $S_9$.
So $S_1 \to S_2, S_3, S_7$.

steps.title: Inside the branches
steps.body: Branch 1: $S_2 \to S_4$. Branch 2: $S_3 \to S_5$ and $S_3 \to S_6$ (inner parbegin), $S_6 \to S_8$. Branch 3: just $S_7$.

steps.title: Join
steps.body:
The outer parend waits for the last statement of each branch — $S_4$, $S_5$, $S_8$ (end of the inner parend) and $S_7$ — so $S_4, S_5, S_8, S_7 \to S_9$.

Edges: $S_1S_2, S_1S_3, S_1S_7, S_2S_4, S_3S_5, S_3S_6, S_6S_8, S_4S_9, S_5S_9, S_8S_9, S_7S_9$.

pitfalls: Reading "S2:S4" as parallel — the colon is a misprinted ";" inside begin…end, i.e. sequence.
Adding an edge S5 → S8: S5 and S6;S8 are parallel branches of the inner parbegin.
cse-1992-b-12-a.verification: Every statement except S1 has at least one predecessor and every statement except S9 at least one successor; 9 nodes, 11 edges.

cse-1992-b-12-b.approach: With window $\Delta = 4$ the working set after reference $t$ is the set of distinct pages among references $t-3 \ldots t$; a reference faults if its page is not in the working set just before it. Tabulate all ten references.
cse-1992-b-12-b.given:
| Item | Value |
|---|---|
| References $t = 1..10$ | c c d b c e c e a d |
| Earlier references | $t=-2$: e, $t=-1$: d, $t=0$: a |
| Window $\Delta$ | 4 |

steps.title: Rule
steps.body: $W(t) = \{$pages referenced at $t-3, t-2, t-1, t\}$. Reference at $t$ faults iff its page $\notin W(t-1)$. $W(0) = \{a, d, e\}$.

steps.title: References 1–5
steps.body:
- $t=1$ c ∉ {a,d,e} → **fault**; window e d a c → {a,c,d,e}, size 4
- $t=2$ c → hit; d a c c → {a,c,d}, 3
- $t=3$ d → hit; a c c d → {a,c,d}, 3
- $t=4$ b → **fault**; c c d b → {b,c,d}, 3
- $t=5$ c → hit; c d b c → {b,c,d}, 3

steps.title: References 6–10
steps.body:

- $t=7$ c → hit; b c e c → {b,c,e}, 3
- $t=8$ e → hit; c e c e → {c,e}, 2
- $t=9$ a → **fault**; e c e a → {a,c,e}, 3

pitfalls: Counting the window as the last 4 distinct pages instead of the last 4 references.
Forgetting that a, d, e from $t \le 0$ are still in the window for the first references.

cse-1992-b-13-a.approach: Each model avoids storing a record twice in its own way: hierarchical via virtual (pointer) records, network via shared owner–member sets, relational via normalization.

steps.title: Hierarchical
steps.body: A child with two parents would be duplicated in two trees; instead a **virtual record / logical pointer** to a single physical copy is stored (IMS logical relationships).

steps.title: Network
steps.body: Records form a graph: a member record is stored **once** and linked to several owners through **set (owner–member) pointers**, so many-to-many links need no copies.

steps.title: Relational
steps.body: Redundancy is removed by **normalization** — decomposing relations (2NF, 3NF, BCNF, …) using functional dependencies, linked by keys/foreign keys.

answer.value: (i) virtual records / logical parent–child pointers instead of duplicate segments; (ii) each record stored once and shared through owner–member set links (pointers); (iii) normalization (decomposition into normal forms)

cse-1992-b-13-a.verification: Each answer names the mechanism by which a single fact is stored in exactly one place in that model.

cse-1992-b-13-b.approach: Select Rama's liked snacks from LIKES, keep only the SNACKS column, join with SERVES on SNACKS, and project HOTEL. FREQUENTS is not needed.

steps.title: Rama's snacks
steps.body: $R_1 = \pi_{SNACKS}\big(\sigma_{CUSTOMER = 'Rama'}(LIKES)\big)$

steps.title: Hotels serving them
steps.body:
$$\pi_{HOTEL}\big(SERVES \bowtie R_1\big) = \pi_{HOTEL}\Big(SERVES \bowtie \pi_{SNACKS}\big(\sigma_{CUSTOMER='Rama'}(LIKES)\big)\Big)$$
The join is on the common attribute SNACKS.

cse-1992-b-14-a.approach: Pair every element with its inverse. Elements that are not self-inverse come in pairs, so the number of self-inverse elements has the same parity as $|G|$, i.e. even; since $e$ is one of them, there is another.

steps.title: Partition G
steps.body: Let $A = \{x \in G : x = x^{-1}\}$ (equivalently $x^2 = e$) and $B = G - A$. For $x \in B$, $x^{-1} \in B$ and $x^{-1} \ne x$, and $(x^{-1})^{-1} = x$, so $B$ splits into disjoint pairs $\{x, x^{-1}\}$ — $|B|$ is even.

steps.title: Count
steps.body: $|A| = |G| - |B|$ = even − even = even. $e \in A$ since $e^2 = e$, so $|A| \ge 1$, hence $|A| \ge 2$: there is $a \in A$ with $a \ne e$ and $a^2 = e$. $\blacksquare$

answer.value: Proved by involution pairing: non-identity elements pair with inverses, leaving at least one element of order 2

pitfalls: Using Cauchy's theorem without proof — valid but the pairing argument is what is expected.
cse-1992-b-14-a.verification: $\mathbb{Z}_4 = \{0,1,2,3\}$: $1 \leftrightarrow 3$ pair up, self-inverse elements are $0$ and $2$; $2 + 2 = 0$ ✓.

cse-1992-b-14-b.approach: The set is the divisor set of 24, closed under LCM and GCD, and these act as join and meet — the defining operations of a lattice. Group/ring/field fail because LCM has no inverses.

steps.title: Lattice
steps.body: $\{1,2,3,4,6,8,12,24\}$ are exactly the divisors of 24. For divisors $a, b$ of 24, $\gcd(a,b)$ and $\operatorname{lcm}(a,b)$ also divide 24 (closure). Both are commutative, associative, idempotent and satisfy absorption ($\operatorname{lcm}(a, \gcd(a,b)) = a$), so $(D_{24}, \operatorname{lcm}, \gcd)$ is a **lattice** (join = lcm, meet = gcd under divisibility).

steps.title: Not a group, ring or field
steps.body: Identity for lcm is 1, but $\operatorname{lcm}(2, x) = 1$ has no solution — no inverses, so not a group. A ring needs an abelian group under its first operation, so it is not a ring and hence not a field.

pitfalls: Calling it a Boolean algebra: 2 has no complement in $D_{24}$ (24 is not square-free).

cse-1992-b-15-a.approach: Convert to clauses and resolve with the substitution $x = a,\ y = a$: get $R(a)$ from (2),(3), then $P(a)$ from (1), which clashes with $\sim P(a)$.

steps.title: Clauses
steps.body: (1) $\sim Q(x) \lor P(x) \lor \sim R(a)$ (2) $R(a) \lor \sim Q(a)$ (3) $Q(a)$ (4) $\sim P(y)$

steps.title: Resolve
steps.body:
- (2) + (3): $R(a)$ … (5)
- (1) with $x = a$ + (3): $P(a) \lor \sim R(a)$ … (6)
- (6) + (5): $P(a)$ … (7)
- (7) + (4) with $y = a$: $\square$ (empty clause)

The empty clause shows the set is **inconsistent**. In modus-ponens form: $Q(a)$ and $Q(a) \rightarrow R(a)$ give $R(a)$; $Q(a)$ and (1) give $P(a) \lor \sim R(a)$, i.e. $R(a) \rightarrow P(a)$, so $P(a)$, contradicting $\forall y\, \sim P(y)$.

answer.value: Derive R(a) from (2),(3); instantiate (1) with x = a to get P(a) ∨ ~R(a), hence P(a); this contradicts ~P(a) from (4) with y = a

pitfalls: Forgetting to instantiate the universally quantified $y$ in (4) with $a$.
cse-1992-b-15-a.verification: Even if (2) were read as R(a) ∧ ~Q(a), ~Q(a) clashes with (3) directly, so the set is inconsistent under either reading.

cse-1992-b-15-b.approach: Check reflexive, symmetric and transitive directly from "$n$ divides $a-b$"; the classes are the residues mod 5.

steps.title: Equivalence
steps.body:
- Reflexive: $a - a = 0 = 0\cdot n$.
- Symmetric: $a - b = kn \Rightarrow b - a = (-k)n$.
- Transitive: $a - b = kn,\ b - c = ln \Rightarrow a - c = (k+l)n$.

steps.title: Classes for n = 5
steps.body:
Every integer is $5k + r$ with $r \in \{0,1,2,3,4\}$, and two integers are related iff they have the same $r$:
$[r] = \{\ldots, r-10, r-5, r, r+5, r+10, \ldots\}$ for $r = 0,1,2,3,4$ — five classes, e.g. $[0] = \{\ldots,-5,0,5,10,\ldots\}$, $[1] = \{\ldots,-4,1,6,\ldots\}$.

answer.value: Five classes: [0], [1], [2], [3], [4] where [r] = {5k + r : k ∈ ℤ}

cse-1992-b-15-b.verification: The five classes are disjoint and cover ℤ (division algorithm), as an equivalence relation's classes must.

cse-1992-b-16.approach: (i) Run the two deciders one after the other. (ii) Pump a prime-length string to a composite length. (iii) Any language is an infinite union of singleton (regular) languages, so closure would make every language regular.

steps.title: (i) True
steps.body: Let $M_1, M_2$ be deciders (always halt) for $L_1, L_2$. On input $w$: run $M_1$; if it accepts, accept; else run $M_2$ and answer as it does. Both halt, so this decides $L_1 \cup L_2$.

steps.title: (ii) True
steps.body: Suppose $L = \{0^p : p \text{ prime}\}$ is regular with pumping length $m$. Pick a prime $p \ge m + 2$, $w = 0^p = xyz$ with $|xy| \le m$, $|y| = k \ge 1$. Pump $i = p - k$: length $= p - k + (p-k)k = (p-k)(k+1)$. Here $k+1 \ge 2$ and $p - k \ge p - m \ge 2$, so the length is composite and $xy^{p-k}z \notin L$ — contradiction.

steps.title: (iii) False
steps.body: Each singleton $\{0^n1^n\}$ is finite, hence regular, but $\bigcup_{n \ge 0}\{0^n1^n\} = \{0^n1^n : n \ge 0\}$ is not regular. (Closure holds only for finite unions.)

pitfalls: Generalising finite-union closure to infinite unions.
In (ii) choosing $i = 0$ or $2$ — that need not give a composite length.
cse-1992-b-16.verification: Concrete check of (ii) with m = 3, p = 5, k = 1: pumped length (5−1)(1+1) = 8, not prime ✓.
